mainTopic: Backing out of a deal: workers who quit, partly paid sales, and when a partial payment acquires
overview: The amud opens by trying to prove that רבי דוסא treats a day-worker and a contractor the same. The proof comes from a ברייתא about a worker forced to stop. רב נחמן בר יצחק rejects it: the ברייתא may be about a דבר האבוד, where everyone agrees. A line in the משנה, 'whoever backs out is at a disadvantage,' then seems to follow רבי דוסא against רב. The גמרא answers two ways. First, רב follows רבי דוסא on only one of his two rules. Second, the line is about a ברייתא on a partly paid field sale. That ברייתא sets out who chooses between money and land when one side backs out, and from what quality of land. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's advice is to write the rest of the price as a loan. A contradiction between his two rulings is settled by רבא's rule: if the seller keeps chasing his money, the buyer does not acquire. The amud ends with a donkey sold with one זוּז still owed, and two clashing traditions from רבא that רב אשי starts to reconcile. That answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: a worker who had to stop still gets paid
steps.stepSummary: The closing words of a ברייתא: a day-worker who was forced to stop gets his wage, and a contractor gets his contract payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: He gives him his wage; if he is a contractor, he gives him his contract payment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its quote of a ברייתא about a worker who had to stop because a relative died or he caught a fever. This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא treats both kinds of workers the same way: a שכיר (paid by time) and a קבלן (paid for the whole job). Both are paid when they are forced to stop. The גמרא will now ask whose opinion this ברייתא follows.

keyTerms.meaning: His wage, the pay of a worker hired by time
A contractor, someone hired to finish a whole job for a set price
His contract payment

phrases.english: he gives him his wage;

phrases.aramaic: אִם קַבְּלָן הוּא – נוֹתֵן לוֹ קַבְּלָנוּתוֹ.
phrases.english: if he is a contractor, he gives him his contract payment.

steps.triggerLanguage: נוֹתֵן לוֹ שְׂכָרוֹ, אִם קַבְּלָן הוּא – נוֹתֵן לוֹ קַבְּלָנוּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the quote of a ברייתא that started before this section.
steps.raayaObject: Whether רבי דוסא distinguishes between שכירות and קבלנות.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a worker who stops because of a death or a fever.

steps.title: The ברייתא cannot follow the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: If this were the רבנן's view, why mention being forced to stop? The רבנן let a worker quit even without a reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is this? If you say the רבנן, why does it speak specifically of one who heard a relative died or caught a fever, meaning he was forced to stop? Even if he was not forced, it should be the same, since the רבנן said the worker has the upper hand!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whose opinion the ברייתא follows. It shows that it cannot be the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן hold יד פועל על העליונה: a worker may quit whenever he wants and still be treated well. So for them there is no reason to talk about a worker who was אנוס (forced). Since the ברייתא does make a point of the worker being forced, it must follow someone stricter.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose opinion is this?
Why specifically this case?
Forced by something outside his control
The worker has the upper hand

phrases.english: Whose opinion is this?
If you say it is the Rabbis,

phrases.aramaic: מַאי אִירְיָא שָׁמַע שֶׁמֵּת לוֹ מֵת
phrases.english: why specifically when he heard that a relative of his died
or a fever gripped him, where he was forced to stop?

for the Rabbis said

steps.triggerLanguage: מַנִּי? אִילֵּימָא רַבָּנַן, מַאי אִירְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks whose opinion the ברייתא from step 1 follows and rules out the רבנן.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the ברייתא follows the רבנן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רבנן let a worker quit even without being forced, so the ברייתא's focus on a forced worker makes no sense for them.

steps.title: So it is רבי דוסא, who treats both workers alike
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא must follow רבי דוסא, so he does not distinguish between a day-worker and a contractor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it רבי דוסא? Learn from this that רבי דוסא makes no difference between hired work and contract work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא concludes that the ברייתא follows רבי דוסא. Since the ברייתא treats both workers alike, so does he.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי דוסא is the one who does not let a worker quit freely, so for him being forced matters. The ברייתא gives the same rule for a שכיר and a קבלן. That shows רבי דוסא applies his rule to both kinds of work.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not...?
Learn from it
Hired work, paid by time
Contract work, paid for the whole job

phrases.english: Rather, is it not Rabbi Dosa's view?
And learn from it
that Rabbi Dosa makes no difference
between hired work and contract work.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו רַבִּי דּוֹסָא הִיא, וּשְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having ruled out the רבנן, it assigns the ברייתא to רבי דוסא and draws the lesson.
steps.raayaObject: רבי דוסא does not distinguish between שכירות and קבלנות.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא, which gives the same rule for a שכיר and a קבלן who are forced to stop.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about work that will be ruined, so everyone agrees
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says the ברייתא is about a דבר האבוד, work where stopping causes a loss, so even the רבנן agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: It is talking about work that will be lost, and it is everyone's opinion.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק rejects the proof. He says the ברייתא can fit everyone, even the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even the רבנן agree that a worker may not freely quit a job where stopping causes a loss. So only a forced worker is treated well there, and the ברייתא's focus on being forced fits the רבנן too. Now nothing is proven about רבי דוסא.

keyTerms.meaning: Work that will be ruined or lost if it is not finished in time
Everyone agrees

steps.confusionAlert: Even the רבנן, who say a worker may quit, agree that in a דבר האבוד he may not walk away without a real reason.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
It is about work that will be lost, and it is everyone's opinion.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: בְּדָבָר הָאָבוּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of steps 2-3 by limiting the ברייתא to a special case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתא must follow רבי דוסא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed an ordinary job. In a דבר האבוד even the רבנן agree, so the ברייתא proves nothing about רבי דוסא.
steps.whatToRemember: The first proof fails: the ברייתא may be about a דבר האבוד, where everyone agrees.

steps.title: A new proof from the משנה: 'whoever backs out loses'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's two rules. It argues the second rule, 'whoever backs out is at a disadvantage,' must be teaching about a worker, following רבי דוסא.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: Whoever changes is at a disadvantage, and whoever backs out is at a disadvantage. The first rule makes sense, since the משנה taught it without a name, following רבי יהודה. But what does 'whoever backs out is at a disadvantage' come to include? Isn't it a worker, following רבי דוסא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new proof by quoting the משנה. It asks what the line about backing out adds, and suggests it adds a worker, following רבי דוסא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first line, 'whoever changes,' is needed because it sets the law like רבי יהודה without naming him. The second line seems extra unless it adds that a worker who backs out loses out, which matches רבי דוסא. That clashes with רב, who ruled like רבי דוסא and yet holds that a worker may quit. The next step answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned in a משנה
The one who changes from what was agreed
The one who backs out of the deal
He is at a disadvantage, he loses out
The תנא taught it to us without naming anyone, which means it is the הלכה
To include, to add another case

phrases.english: We learned in the Mishnah:
Whoever changes is at a disadvantage,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל הַחוֹזֵר בּוֹ יָדוֹ עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה.
phrases.english: and whoever backs out is at a disadvantage.

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁלָמָא כׇּל הַמְשַׁנֶּה יָדוֹ עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה,

phrases.notes: Earlier in the משנה, רבי יהודה ruled that the one who changes from the deal loses out.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כׇּל הַחוֹזֵר בּוֹ יָדוֹ עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה
phrases.english: But 'whoever backs out is at a disadvantage,'
what does it come to include?
Isn't it to include a worker,
and following Rabbi Dosa?

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: כׇּל הַמְשַׁנֶּה יָדוֹ עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was rejected, the גמרא tries a new proof from the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That the משנה's unnamed ruling follows רבי דוסא: a worker who backs out loses out.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The extra line in the משנה: 'whoever backs out is at a disadvantage.'
steps.whyThisMatters: An unnamed משנה usually sets the הלכה. If this line follows רבי דוסא, the הלכה may follow him against the רבנן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that a worker may quit, given that רב also rules like רבי דוסא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the משנה's extra line adds a worker, then the unnamed משנה follows רבי דוסא, who says a worker who backs out loses out. That contradicts רב's view that a worker may quit.

steps.title: רב agrees with רבי דוסא on one rule and disagrees on the other
steps.stepSummary: רבי דוסא taught two separate rules. רב accepts one of them and rejects the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי דוסא is saying two separate things. רב holds like him on one of them and argues with him on the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers how רב can rule like רבי דוסא and yet hold that a worker may quit. It splits רבי דוסא's words into two separate rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 read 'whoever backs out is at a disadvantage' as רבי דוסא's rule against a worker who quits. That clashes with רב's view that a worker may quit. The answer is that רבי דוסא gave two rules: one about how to work out the wage, and one penalizing a worker who backs out. רב follows him on the wage calculation but rejects the penalty on the worker.

keyTerms.meaning: He is saying two separate things
He holds like him
In one matter
He disagrees with him

steps.confusionAlert: Ruling 'like' a תנא does not have to mean agreeing with everything he said. Here רב accepts only part of רבי דוסא's teaching.

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Dosa is saying two things,
and Rav holds like him in one,
phrases.notes: This is the rule about how to work out the worker's pay.

phrases.english: and disagrees with him in one.
phrases.notes: This is the rule that a worker who backs out loses out. רב lets a worker quit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא רַבִּי דּוֹסָא תַּרְתֵּי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the clash created by Step 5's reading of the משנה against רב's ruling.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting one opinion into two independent rulings
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since רב follows רבי דוסא, he must also agree that a worker who quits loses out.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב adopts רבי דוסא's wage calculation only, not his penalty on a quitting worker.

steps.title: A second reading: the phrase is about a land sale
steps.stepSummary: The phrase 'whoever backs out is at a disadvantage' points to a ברייתא about a partly paid field sale. If the seller backs out, the buyer has the upper hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say this instead: 'Whoever backs out is at a disadvantage' refers to a ברייתא. How so? Someone sold a field for 1,000 זוז, and the buyer paid 200 זוז. If the seller backs out, the buyer has the upper hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer. The phrase in the משנה is not about workers at all. It refers to a ברייתא about selling a field, and the גמרא starts quoting it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the phrase is not about workers, it cannot be used to show that רבי דוסא penalizes a worker who quits. The ברייתא's case is a sale where only part of the money was paid. Here the seller backed out, so the buyer is the one who gets to choose the outcome.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say; it introduces another possible answer
Whoever backs out of a deal
He is at a disadvantage (literally, his hand is on the bottom)
Has the upper hand
A silver coin

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
"Whoever backs out is at a disadvantage,"
phrases.notes: This is the second rule from the משנה, the one quoted in Step 5.

phrases.english: refers to what is taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי שֶׁמָּכַר שָׂדֶה לַחֲבֵירוֹ בְּאֶלֶף זוּז,
phrases.english: If one sold a field to his fellow for a thousand zuz,

When the seller backs out,

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different way out of the problem that Step 6 solved.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the phrase as being about a different case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase in the משנה is about a worker who quits.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase is about a buyer or seller who backs out of a partly paid land sale.

steps.title: Who chooses, and which land is used
steps.stepSummary: The side that did not back out gets to choose: a refund, or land worth the 200. If the seller backed out, he pays from his best land. If the buyer backed out, the seller may pay from his worst land.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the seller backed out, the buyer may say 'Give me my money back' or 'Give me land worth my money.' The seller must pay from his best land. If the buyer backed out, the seller has the upper hand. He may say 'Here is your money' or 'Here is land worth your money,' and he may pay from his worst land.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and explains what 'upper hand' means in practice, first when the seller backs out and then when the buyer backs out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The side that kept its word gets to choose between a refund and land worth the 200 זוז. Even the type of land depends on who backed out. The seller who backed out must give his best land, but if the buyer backed out, the seller may give his worst land. This shows clearly how the one who backs out is at a disadvantage.

keyTerms.meaning: Land equal in value to my money
He pays him (collects for him)
Best-quality land
Worst-quality land
Here, take it

steps.whatToRemember: Whoever backs out of the sale loses the choice. The other side picks between money and land, and the type of land is decided in that other side's favor.

phrases.english: If he wants, he says to him: "Give me my money,"
or: "Give me land equal to my money."
From where does he pay him? From the best land.
And when the buyer backs out,
the seller has the upper hand:
if he wants, he says to him: "Here is your money,"
if he wants, he says: "Here is land equal to your money."
From where does he pay him? From the worst land.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָצָה אוֹמֵר לוֹ תֵּן לִי מְעוֹתַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the ברייתא and spells out what 'upper hand' means.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The side that kept its word chooses between a refund and land worth the payment. A seller who backs out pays from his best land; when the buyer backs out, the seller may pay from his worst land.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: turn the balance into a loan
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says to stop backing out from the start. The seller writes that the field is sold and the buyer owes 800 זוז, so the sale is final and the rest is a debt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: we teach them how to keep the deal from falling apart. The seller writes: 'I, so-and-so, sold this field to so-and-so for 1,000 זוז. He paid me 200, and he owes me 800.' The buyer then owns the field and can pay the rest even years later.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's advice for preventing the problem altogether: write the unpaid balance as a debt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the document says the field is sold and the buyer owes 800 זוז, the sale is complete. The buyer acquires the field right away. The unpaid part becomes an ordinary loan, so neither side can back out, and the buyer may pay it off even after many years.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who adds his own view in the ברייתא
We teach them how not to back out
So-and-so
He owes me (literally, I am his creditor)
He has acquired it

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a practical way to make a partly paid sale final: write the remaining balance as a loan.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
We teach them not to back out. How so?
He writes for him:
phrases.notes: The seller is the one writing the document for the buyer.

phrases.english: "I, so-and-so son of so-and-so,

phrases.aramaic: מָכַרְתִּי שָׂדֶה פְּלוֹנִית לִפְלוֹנִי בְּאֶלֶף זוּז,
phrases.english: sold such-and-such field to so-and-so for a thousand zuz,
and he gave me two hundred zuz of them,

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲרֵינִי נוֹשֶׁה בּוֹ שְׁמוֹנֶה מֵאוֹת זוּז״,
phrases.english: and he owes me eight hundred zuz,"
he acquires the field, and pays him the rest,
even after several years.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר מְלַמְּדִין אוֹתָן שֶׁלֹּא יַחְזְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא with a way to stop either side from backing out.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the seller writes the unpaid balance as a debt, the buyer acquires the field at once and repays the rest as a loan, even years later.

steps.title: Re-quoting the rule that the seller pays from his best land
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's line that the seller pays from עידית, and first assumes this means the best land of all his property.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: From where does he pay? From the best land. You might think this means the best land of all his property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the ברייתא in step 8 and states how we would first understand it. This is a setup: the גמרא is about to attack this understanding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 8 the ברייתא said that if the seller backed out, the buyer gets paid from the best land (עידית). The first reading is that this means the best land out of everything the seller owns. That is the reading the next step will challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: "The Master said." The גמרא is quoting an earlier source, here the ברייתא.
He pays him, by giving him land to collect
The best quality land
"It enters your mind." This marks a first assumption the גמרא will question.

phrases.english: The Master said: From where does he pay him?
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא from step 8, about the seller who backed out.

phrases.english: From the best land.
It enters your mind to say
from the best land of all his property.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: מֵהֵיכָן מַגְבֵּיהוּ? מִן הָעִידִּית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא of step 8 to look more closely at the word עידית.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא says the seller who backed out pays from עידית. At first we assume this means the best of all his property.

steps.title: Why should the buyer get better land than a creditor?
steps.stepSummary: Even a regular creditor only collects medium land, and the buyer paid for one specific field, so why should he get the seller's best land?
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him be no worse off than a regular creditor! But we learned that a creditor collects from medium land. And also, there is the specific field he paid money for!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first reading with two problems.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First problem: a regular lender (בעל חוב) only collects from medium land (בינונית), so the buyer should get no more than that. Second problem: the buyer paid for one particular field, so why should he get land from the seller's other fields at all?

keyTerms.meaning: A creditor, someone who is owed money
Medium quality land
"And we learned," quoting a משנה
"And furthermore," adding a second problem

phrases.english: Let him be no more than a creditor!
phrases.notes: He means: at most, the buyer is owed money like any lender.

phrases.english: And we learned: a creditor's right is to medium land.
And furthermore: there is this land that he paid money for?
phrases.notes: He means the one field the buyer actually paid toward. Why take from a different field?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא יְהֵא אֶלָּא בַּעַל חוֹב

steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that עידית means the best of all the seller's property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A creditor only gets בינונית, and the buyer's claim is tied to one specific field, so giving him the best of everything makes no sense.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: the best or worst part of that same field
steps.stepSummary: עידית means the best part of the field being sold, and זיבורית means the worst part of that same field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: from the best land within it, and from the worst land within it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers by reading the ברייתא as talking only about the field being sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The best land and worst land in step 8 are both parts of the field being sold, not the seller's other fields. This answers both problems. The buyer stays within the field he paid for, and he is not getting the seller's best property in general.

keyTerms.meaning: The worst quality land
"That is in it," meaning inside the field being sold

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
From the best land that is in it,
and from the worst land that is in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: מֵעִידִּית שֶׁבָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source: limiting it to the field being sold
steps.terutzHavaAmina: עידית means the best of all the seller's property.
steps.terutzMaskana: עידית and זיבורית mean the best and worst parts of the field being sold.

steps.title: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא: the buyer is like an injured party
steps.stepSummary: Even if it means the best of all the seller's property, that is fair, because the buyer usually sold his own things cheaply to raise the money. That makes him like a ניזק, and a ניזק is paid from עידית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא said: you can even say it means the best of all his property. Usually someone buying land for a thousand זוז sells his own belongings cheaply to raise the money, so he is like an injured party. And we learned: injured parties are paid from the best land.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives a different answer. He keeps the first reading and explains why it is fair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא accepts that the buyer gets the best of all the seller's property. The reason is that the buyer is not a simple lender. To raise a large sum, he probably sold his own belongings at a loss, so the seller who backs out has actually caused him damage. That puts him in the category of a ניזק, and the משנה says a ניזק is paid from עידית.

keyTerms.meaning: "You can even say," keeping the first reading after all
He sells cheaply, at a real loss
An injured party, someone who was damaged
They assess, meaning בית דין values the land for payment

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two answers. רב נחמן בר יצחק says the land comes from the sold field itself. רב אחא says it really is the best of all the seller's property, because the buyer counts as a ניזק and not as a regular בעל חוב.
steps.whatToRemember: Two answers: (1) עידית and זיבורית are parts of the field being sold. (2) The buyer is like a ניזק, so he collects from the seller's best land overall.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Acha, son of Rav Ika, said:
You can even say it means from the best land of all his property,

phrases.aramaic: סְתַם מַאן דְּזָבֵין אַרְעָא בְּאַלְפָּא זוּזֵי –
phrases.english: since ordinarily, someone who buys land for a thousand zuz
sells his own property very cheaply to raise the money,
and so he is like an injured party.
And we learned: for injured parties, they assess payment from the best land.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא מֵעִידִּית דִּנְכָסָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 11, different from step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Putting the buyer in a different category: ניזק instead of בעל חוב
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer is like a בעל חוב and should only get בינונית.
steps.terutzMaskana: The buyer is like a ניזק, who collects from עידית of all the seller's property.

steps.title: Re-quoting רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's contract wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבן שמעון בן גמליאל again: we teach them not to back out by having the seller write a contract.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: we teach them not to back out. How? He writes for him: "I, so-and-so, son of so-and-so," and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ruling from step 9 again. This is a setup: it is preparing to ask a question about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No new rule is added here. The גמרא repeats רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's words so it can look closely at what they imply in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: We teach them, meaning we guide the parties on what to do
So that they will not back out
So-and-so, son of so-and-so

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
We teach them not to back out.
How? He writes for him:
"I, so-and-so, son of so-and-so," etc.
phrases.notes: "Etc." points to the full wording from step 9: the field is sold, and the buyer owes 800 זוז.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: מְלַמְּדִין אוֹתָן שֶׁלֹּא יַחְזְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ruling from step 9 so it can examine it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing that the field is sold and the rest is a debt makes the sale final.

steps.title: Does the buyer acquire only because of the contract?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers that the sale is final only because of this wording, which would mean the buyer does not acquire without it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is that he wrote this for him. So if he did not write this, the buyer does not acquire?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's words and questions it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the contract wording is what makes the sale final, then a partial payment alone would not let the buyer acquire the field. The גמרא raises this as a surprising result that needs explaining.

keyTerms.meaning: "The reason is," introducing an inference
"But if not," the flip side of the inference
He acquires

phrases.english: The reason is that he wrote this for him,
so if he did not write this,
he does not acquire?

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דִּכְתַב לֵיהּ הָכִי, הָא לָא כְּתַב הָכִי – לָא קָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the ruling quoted in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: What רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling implies
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the special wording is needed, then partial payment alone does not let the buyer acquire, and that conclusion needs explaining.

steps.title: A ברייתא about a down payment with conditions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins quoting a ברייתא about a down payment where each side sets a penalty for backing out. רבי יוסי says the conditions stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: Someone gives a down payment to another and says, 'If I back out, my down payment is yours.' The other one says, 'If I back out, I will pay you double your down payment.' The conditions stand. This is the opinion of רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge by starting to quote a ברייתא. The part that actually challenges the earlier quote comes a little later, from רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes a buyer and a seller who each agree to a penalty for backing out. רבי יוסי rules that these penalties are binding. This opens the ברייתא whose later lines will clash with the earlier quote of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא? This phrase introduces a source that challenges what was just said.
A down payment, meaning part of the price paid up front.
I back out of the deal.
I will double it.
The conditions stand, so the court enforces them.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: one who gives a down payment to his fellow
and says to him: 'If I back out,
my down payment is forgiven to you,'
and the other says: 'If I back out,
I will double your down payment for you' –
the conditions stand; these are the words of רבי יוסי.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that will challenge the reading in Step 15, where the sale was final only because of the written contract.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier quote of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, as read in Step 15: without a written contract, the buyer does not acquire.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This is the opening of the ברייתא. Its later lines show רבן שמעון בן גמליאל saying that partial payment acquires even with no contract.

steps.title: רבי יוסי holds that an אסמכתא works
steps.stepSummary: A side comment: רבי יוסי rules this way because he holds that a promise made under an אסמכתא is binding.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי follows his usual view, because he says that an אסמכתא acquires.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses the ברייתא to explain why רבי יוסי lets the penalties stand. He holds that an אסמכתא is binding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each side made his promise sure that he would never back out, so the promise is an אסמכתא. Many say such a promise is not seriously meant. רבי יוסי holds that it is still a real, binding commitment, and that is why he enforces the conditions.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own usual reasoning.
A promise someone makes because he is confident he will never have to keep it.
It acquires, meaning it is legally binding.

phrases.english: רבי יוסי follows his own reasoning,
for he says: an אסמכתא acquires.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי לְטַעְמֵיהּ דְּאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side note explaining the reasoning behind רבי יוסי's ruling in Step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוסי holds that an אסמכתא is binding, so the penalty conditions are enforced.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: half payment acquires the whole field
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. רבי יהודה limits the down payment to acquiring only its own value. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that in a normal sale, paying half the price acquires the whole field. This contradicts the earlier quote.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: It is enough for the down payment to acquire only as much as its own value. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: When does this apply? When the buyer said, 'Let my down payment acquire.' But if someone sold a field for a thousand זוז and the buyer paid him five hundred, he acquires the field. He pays back the rest even after several years!
steps.whatsHappening: Here is the actual challenge. In this ברייתא, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that paying half the price acquires the whole field with no contract at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, in Step 15, it looked as if רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that the buyer acquires only if a contract was written. Here he says that half payment acquires the whole field, and the rest simply becomes money owed. So the two quotes from the same תנא seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: It is enough for him.
As much as his down payment is worth.
In what case are these words said? This phrase limits a ruling to a certain case.
Let it acquire.
The rest of the money still owed.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבן שמעון בן גמליאל is disagreeing with himself on purpose. The גמרא is about to show that he is talking about a different case here.

phrases.english: רבי יהודה says:
It is enough that he acquires as much as his down payment.
רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said:
In what case are these words said?
When he said to him: 'Let my down payment acquire.'

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מָכַר לוֹ שָׂדֶה בְּאֶלֶף זוּז
phrases.english: But if he sold him a field for a thousand זוז

phrases.aramaic: וְנָתַן לוֹ מֵהֶם חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת זוּז – קָנָה,
phrases.english: and the buyer gave him five hundred of them, he has acquired,
phrases.notes: He acquires the whole field, not just half of it.

phrases.english: and he gives him the rest
even after several years!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל מָכַר לוֹ שָׂדֶה בְּאֶלֶף זוּז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא begun in Step 16 and makes the challenge against Step 15 explicit.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that, according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, the buyer acquires only with a written contract.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In this ברייתא, the same רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that half payment acquires the whole field without any contract. So a contract should not be needed.

steps.title: It depends on whether the seller is visibly looking for money
steps.stepSummary: The two rulings deal with different cases. If the seller is running around looking for money, a contract is needed. If he is not, half payment acquires.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This ruling is where he is going in and out looking for money. That ruling is where he is not going in and out looking for money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction by splitting the two rulings into two different situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the seller is clearly hunting for cash, he sold the field because he needs the full price now. So paying only half does not finish the sale unless a contract turned the rest into a loan. If he is not hunting for cash, he is fine with waiting, so half payment acquires and the rest is simply money owed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. This phrase introduces an answer that splits the cases.
He goes in and out for money, meaning he shows he urgently needs cash.

steps.whatToRemember: A partial payment acquires the whole field and turns the rest into money owed, unless the seller shows he urgently needs cash. In that case, a written contract is needed for the buyer to acquire before paying in full.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule: the seller's visible need for money decides whether a partial payment finishes the sale.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is where he goes in and goes out for money,
phrases.notes: "This" is the earlier ruling that needed a written contract, and "he" is the seller.

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּלָא קָא עָיֵיל וְנָפֵיק אַזּוּזֵי.
phrases.english: that is where he does not go in and go out for money.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דְּקָא עָיֵיל וְנָפֵיק אַזּוּזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in Step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the two rulings apply to different situations.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two quotes of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל seemed to clash about whether a contract is needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: A contract is needed only when the seller is clearly looking for money. Otherwise, half payment acquires the whole field.

steps.title: רבא's source for the distinction
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if the seller keeps chasing after his money, the buyer does not acquire. If he does not chase it, the buyer acquires.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבא says: if someone sells something to his friend and then keeps going in and out looking for money, the buyer has not acquired it. If he does not go in and out for money, the buyer has acquired it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ruling of רבא to back up the answer it just gave in step 19.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 said the outcome depends on whether the seller is running around for money. רבא's ruling says exactly that. A seller who keeps chasing his money shows he sold only because he needed cash right away, so without full payment the sale does not take hold.

keyTerms.meaning: goes in and goes out, meaning he keeps running around
for money (literally, for the coins)
he acquires; the purchase takes effect
something, an item

phrases.english: As רבא says:
One who sells something to his friend
and keeps going in and out for money —
phrases.notes: He means the seller keeps chasing after the money he is still owed.

phrases.english: the buyer has not acquired.
If he does not go in and out for money —
the buyer has acquired.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source that supports the distinction drawn in step 19.
steps.raayaObject: The answer in step 19: a seller who runs around for money needs a contract, and if he does not, half payment acquires.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's ruling that chasing after money means the buyer does not acquire.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling becomes the base for the case of the donkey and the single זוּז that follows.

steps.title: Paying back a loan one coin at a time
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that paying back a loan of one hundred זוּזים one coin at a time counts as repayment, but the lender has a fair complaint.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא says: if someone lent one hundred זוּזים to his friend and the friend paid him back one זוּז at a time, it counts as repayment. But the lender has a complaint against him, because he can say: you wasted it on me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another ruling of רבא about paying in small pieces, as a side point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The debt is fully paid, so legally nothing is wrong. Still, small coins tend to get spent one by one, while a lump sum can be used for something meaningful, so the lender has a moral complaint.

keyTerms.meaning: who lent him
repayment
a complaint or grievance
you caused them to be lost or wasted

phrases.english: And רבא says:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי מַאן דְּאוֹזְפֵיהּ מְאָה זוּזֵי לְחַבְרֵיהּ
phrases.english: One who lent one hundred זוּזים to his friend
and the friend paid him back one זוּז at a time —
it is a valid repayment,
but the lender has a complaint against him,
since he can say to him: You wasted it on me.
phrases.notes: Coins that come in one at a time slip away; a lump sum could have been put to real use.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ruling of רבא, brought next to the first because both deal with getting money in small amounts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Paying a loan back coin by coin is valid repayment, but the lender has a fair complaint.

steps.title: The donkey sale with one זוּז still owed
steps.stepSummary: A man sold his donkey and was still owed one זוּז, and he kept chasing after it. רב אשי asks whether the buyer acquired.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who sold his donkey to his friend, and one זוּז was still owed to him, and he kept going in and out for that זוּז. רב אשי sat and thought it through: in a case like this, what is the law? Did the buyer acquire or not?
steps.whatsHappening: A real case comes up, and רב אשי asks how רבא's rule applies when only one coin is still missing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said that chasing after money cancels the sale. The question is whether chasing after just one זוּז is enough to show the seller badly needed the cash, or whether such a small amount does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: a donkey
remained, was still owed
examining, thinking it through
in a case like this

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּזַבֵּין לֵיהּ חֲמָרָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ
phrases.english: A certain man sold his donkey to his friend
and one זוּז was still owed to him,
and he kept going in and out for that זוּז.

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב רַב אָשֵׁי וְקָא מְעַיֵּין בַּהּ:
phrases.english: רב אשי sat and thought it through:
In a case like this, what is the law?
Did the buyer acquire, or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּזַבֵּין לֵיהּ חֲמָרָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבא's rule from step 20 to an edge case where only one coin is missing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does chasing after a single remaining זוּז cancel the sale the way chasing after a larger amount does?

steps.title: One זוּז counts like many
steps.stepSummary: רב מרדכי quotes רבא through אבימי מהגרוניא: one זוּז is treated like many, so the buyer has not acquired.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרדכי said to רב אשי: this is what אבימי from הגרוניא said in the name of רבא: one זוּז is like many זוּזים, and the buyer has not acquired.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרדכי answers רב אשי's question with a tradition from רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a single coin, if the seller keeps chasing it, shows he wanted all his money before giving up the item. So the small amount makes no difference, and the sale does not take hold.

keyTerms.meaning: one זוּז is like many זוּזים
in the name of
this is what he said

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב מָרְדֳּכַי לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: רב מרדכי said to רב אשי:

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי אָמַר אֲבִימִי מֵהַגְרוֹנְיָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא:
phrases.english: This is what אבימי from הגרוניא said in the name of רבא:
One זוּז is like many זוּזים,
and the buyer has not acquired.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב מָרְדֳּכַי לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's question from step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Chasing even one זוּז counts as chasing money, so the buyer does not acquire.

steps.title: A different tradition from רבא
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב יוסף objects that רבא was quoted as ruling that the buyer does acquire.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא, son of רב יוסף, said to רב אשי: but we say in the name of רבא that the buyer has acquired!
steps.whatsHappening: Another sage pushes back with a version of רבא's ruling that says the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there are two traditions in רבא's name about the same kind of case: one says the buyer did not acquire, the other says he did. One of them seems to be wrong unless they are talking about different cases.

keyTerms.meaning: but we say, an objection from a known tradition

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יוֹסֵף לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: רב אחא, son of רב יוסף, said to רב אשי:
But we say in the name of רבא that he has acquired!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אָמְרִינַן מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא קָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the tradition quoted in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב מרדכי's version of רבא: one זוּז is like many, so the buyer does not acquire.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A different tradition in רבא's name says the buyer does acquire, so the two quotes contradict each other.

steps.title: The other version is about selling a field
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי begins to answer: the tradition saying the buyer acquires should be read as talking about someone who sells his field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to him: explain your teaching as talking about someone who sells his field...
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי begins to settle the contradiction by saying the two traditions are about different cases. The sentence continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of throwing out one tradition, רב אשי says the version that rules 'he acquired' was said about selling a field. That leaves room for רב מרדכי's version to stay true for a case like the donkey.

keyTerms.meaning: explain it, interpret it
your teaching, the tradition you heard
one who sells his field

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not saying רב אחא's tradition is wrong. He is placing it in a different case, a field sale, so both traditions can be true.

phrases.english: רב אשי said to him:
Explain your teaching as talking about one who sells his field

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּתַּרְגַּם שְׁמַעְתָּיךָ בְּמוֹכֵר שָׂדֵהוּ
